Live production compared

vMix vs Wirecast: two ways to switch live video

By Syd Lawrence, a visual artist and developer who makes Vibresia. Facts last checked 2 November 2026; updated 2 November 2026.

If you are on Windows and want the cheaper way in, pick vMix: Basic HD is US$60 once, and there is a 60-day trial of the full Pro edition. If you need it on a Mac as well, or want remote guests, ISO recording or sports tools, pick Wirecast, which runs on both and is US$59 a month. The platform difference settles more than the price does: there is no macOS version of vMix, as it cannot be installed directly on OSX and can only be installed on Windows via Boot Camp on older Intel Macs.

Control and connections

vMixWirecast
MIDIYes: vMix accepts MIDI from controllers for shortcuts, and can send MIDI out to lights and faders through its Activators feature.Yes: Wirecast reads MIDI control surface input from named controllers rather than sending MIDI out, with the user guide listing APC MINI, APC40mk2, Launchpad MK2 and XKeys 128.
SyphonNo: vMix has no Syphon input or output, because there is no macOS version of vMix, and Mac sources reach vMix through NDI or OMT scan converters instead.No: Wirecast removed Syphon as a source option in version 14.0 because it moved to the Metal rendering framework, and the current user guide lists no Syphon source or output.
NDIYes: vMix receives NDI sources from the network and sends its output over NDI, with up to four independently configurable NDI outputs in the 4K, Pro and Max editions.Yes: NDI input works on both Mac and Windows in every version, and Wirecast Pro can additionally send its programme feed out over NDI.
Video in and outYes: vMix ingests video from cameras, capture cards, video files, NDI, OMT and SRT, and outputs it by recording, streaming and sending it to monitors and other machines.Yes: Wirecast sends video out through a virtual camera, streaming destinations, NDI programme output, baseband SDI or HDMI cards, secondary display, and records to disk.

Every row comes from the app's own documentation, on the date shown in the sources below. "Not that we could find" means we could not find it documented, not that the app cannot do it.

Pick vMix if

you are on Windows, you want to pay once rather than every month, and you need instant replay or remote callers. Basic HD is US$60 once, the full edition is US$50 a month, and the trial runs the Pro edition for 60 days.

Pick Wirecast if

you need it on a Mac as well as Windows, you want ISO recording of each camera feed, or you need sports production tools and PTZ camera control. Studio is US$59 a month and Pro is US$79.

Why people compare them

They are the two paid live production switchers that come up together, because they do the same job: mix cameras and other sources, and send the result out as a stream, a recording and a feed to other machines.

vMix is a live video production and streaming switcher for windows that mixes cameras, network sources and media, then records and streams the result. Wirecast is live video production software for mac and windows that switches cameras, mixes sources and streams or records the result. The interesting part is not the feature list, it is that one of them does not run on the computer half the people reading this own.

Where vMix wins

It costs less to get into. US$60, one-time once for Basic HD, and one-off licences at US$350, one-time, US$700, one-time and US$1,200, one-time above it, each with twelve months of free version updates. The subscription is US$50 a month a month for the full edition.

Its trial is the better one. the trial lasts 60 days and runs vMix Pro with all its features, including 4K, MultiCorder and full Instant Replay. A paid licence is needed after the 60 days.

It has instant replay. Handles remote guests with vMix Call for up to eight callers, and slow-motion instant replay for up to eight cameras

It sends its output to other machines. Sends program output to other machines over NDI, with up to four independently configurable NDI outputs in the 4K, Pro and Max editions

Where Wirecast wins

It runs on a Mac. Wirecast is listed for Windows, Mac. there is no macOS version of vMix, as it cannot be installed directly on OSX and can only be installed on Windows via Boot Camp on older Intel Macs.

Its free download is unlimited. the free download is a fully functional trial of Studio and Pro with no time limit and no credit card needed, but every output and recording carries a visual and audio watermark until a valid licence is purchased and activated, and the user guide adds that a Studio licence used with a Pro feature watermarks just that Pro output.

It records each camera separately. Wirecast records the programme mix to disk while streaming, and Pro adds ISO recording that saves each camera feed as its own file plus multi-track audio recording

Remote guests need no download. Rendezvous brings remote guests into the production as browser-based calls, so Studio supports 2 guests and Pro supports 7, with no software download needed on the guest side

It has sports tools. NDI input works in every version and on both platforms, and Wirecast Pro can also broadcast its programme feed back out over NDI

Where both fall short

Neither is free to run. the cheapest edition, Basic HD at 60 dollars, is limited to four total inputs, three of them cameras or NDI, 1920 by 1080 output and one overlay channel, and it leaves out vMix Call, MultiCorder, Instant Replay, scripting, PTZ control, the Mix input and the extra outputs. the free trial is unlimited in time but watermarks every output and recording, with a periodic Wirecast logo overlay on the video and a periodic voice-over on the audio.

Both are subscriptions once you are past the trial. vMix has one-off licences but they carry twelve months of free version updates and nothing after that, and Wirecast's pricing page lists no one-time or perpetual purchase at all.

Both cap what you can drive. recording is capped at two recorders, and four external outputs, two fullscreen outputs and four virtual outputs come only with the 4K, Pro and Max editions. And even in Wirecast Pro, the video output carries only two audio channels, so a baseband SDI connection cannot deliver the 16 channels the SDI standard supports.

Neither is a music visualiser. Both are general tools for video, and both expect you to bring the content. If what you want is visuals that react to what the Mac is playing, with nothing to prepare, that is a different job than either of these does.

What it costs

vMix has one-off licences from US$60, one-time for Basic HD up to US$1,200, one-time for Pro, and a subscription at US$50 a month a month for the full edition.

Wirecast Studio is US$59 a month a month, or US$34 a month a month when billed yearly, which the price page says saves 300 dollars a year. Wirecast Pro is US$79 a month a month, or US$42 a month a month billed yearly. Both charge in US dollars, so the rate on the day you buy is yours to check.

Questions people ask

Does vMix run on a Mac?

No. There is no macOS version of vMix, as it cannot be installed directly on OSX and can only be installed on Windows via Boot Camp on older Intel Macs. Wirecast runs on Windows, Mac, so on a Mac it is the one that works.

Which is cheaper, vMix or Wirecast?

vMix's entry point is US$60 once, though Basic HD is limited to three camera inputs and 1080p. Wirecast Studio is US$59 a month, or US$34 a month billed yearly.

Can I try either one for free?

Yes. the trial lasts 60 days and runs vMix Pro with all its features, including 4K, MultiCorder and full Instant Replay. A paid licence is needed after the 60 days. the free download is a fully functional trial of Studio and Pro with no time limit and no credit card needed, but every output and recording carries a visual and audio watermark until a valid licence is purchased and activated, and the user guide adds that a Studio licence used with a Pro feature watermarks just that Pro output.

Which one records each camera separately?

Wirecast Pro. Its ISO recording saves each camera feed as its own file, with multi-track audio recording of up to eight stereo tracks. vMix has MultiCorder, which the trial includes, but it is a Pro feature rather than a Studio one.
